content: Demadex tablets are available for oral administration and contain the active ingredient torsemide. For detailed information about torsemide, you can refer to the provided resources. Adverse Reactions Adverse reactions associated with Demadex include polyuria (excessive urination) and rhinitis (inflammation of the nasal mucosa). Adult Indications and Dosage 1. Chronic Renal Failure Edema: The usual initial dose is 20 mg of oral Demadex once daily. If the diuretic response is inadequate, the dose should be titrated upward by approximately doubling until the desired diuretic effect is achieved. Single doses higher than 200 mg have not been adequately studied. 2. Congestive Heart Failure Edema: The usual initial dose is 10 mg or 20 mg of oral Demadex once daily. If the diuretic response is inadequate, the dose should be titrated upward by approximately doubling until the desired diuretic effect is achieved. Single doses higher than 200 mg have not been adequately studied. 3. Hepatic Disease Edema: The usual initial dose is 5 mg or 10 mg of oral Demadex once daily, administered with an aldosterone antagonist or a potassium-sparing diuretic. If the diuretic response is inadequate, the dose should be titrated upward by approximately doubling until the desired diuretic effect is achieved. Single doses higher than 40 mg have not been adequately studied. Chronic use of diuretics in hepatic disease has not been studied in well-controlled trials. 4. Hypertension: The usual initial dose is 5 mg once daily. If the 5 mg dose does not provide adequate blood pressure reduction within 4 to 6 weeks, the dose may be increased to 10 mg once daily. If the response to 10 mg is insufficient, an additional antihypertensive agent should be added to the treatment regimen. Pediatric Indications and Dosage The safety and effectiveness of Demadex in pediatric patients have not been established. Administration of other loop diuretics to severely premature infants with edema due to patent ductus arteriosus and hyaline membrane disease has occasionally been associated with renal calcifications, sometimes visible on X-ray or in staghorn form. In some cases, these calculi have dissolved, and hypercalciuria has decreased when chlorothiazide was coadministered with the loop diuretic. The use of Demadex in such patients has not been studied. Contraindications Demadex is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to torsemide or sulfonylureas. It is also contraindicated in patients who are anuric (unable to produce urine). Warnings 1. Hepatic Disease with Cirrhosis and Ascites: Use Demadex cautiously in patients with hepatic disease, as sudden alterations in fluid and electrolyte balance may precipitate hepatic coma. Diuresis with Demadex should ideally be initiated in a hospital setting. To prevent hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, an aldosterone antagonist or potassium-sparing drug should be used concomitantly. 2. Ototoxicity: Tinnitus and hearing loss (usually reversible) have been observed after rapid intravenous injection of other loop diuretics and oral Demadex. These events may not be directly attributable to Demadex. Ototoxicity has also been observed in animal studies at very high plasma levels of torsemide. Intravenous Demadex should be injected slowly over 2 minutes, and single doses should not exceed 200 mg. 3. Volume and Electrolyte Depletion: Patients receiving diuretics should be monitored for signs of electrolyte imbalance, hypovolemia, or prerenal azotemia. Symptoms may include dryness of the mouth, thirst, weakness, lethargy, drowsiness, restlessness, muscle pain or cramps, muscular fatigue, hypotension, oliguria, tachycardia, nausea, and vomiting. Excessive diuresis may lead to dehydration, blood volume reduction, and possibly thrombosis or embolism, especially in elderly patients. If fluid and electrolyte imbalances occur, Demadex should be discontinued until corrected and restarted at a lower dose. Drug Interactions Demadex has been coadministered with beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, calcium-channel blockers, digitalis glycosides, and organic nitrates without new or unexpected adverse events. Torsemide does not affect the protein binding of glyburide or warfarin, nor the pharmacokinetics of digoxin or carvedilol. High doses of salicylates may lead to salicylate toxicity when coadministered with Demadex. The natriuretic effect of Demadex may be partially inhibited by indomethacin under conditions of dietary sodium restriction. Coadministration with cholestyramine may reduce the absorption of orally administered torsemide. Lithium toxicity risk may increase when coadministered with diuretics, including Demadex. Overdose Signs of overdose may include dehydration, hypovolemia, hypotension, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypochloremic alkalosis, and hemoconcentration. Treatment should focus on fluid and electrolyte replacement. Torsemide is not dialyzable, so hemodialysis will not accelerate elimination. Pharmacology Torsemide acts within the lumen of the thick ascending loop of Henle, inhibiting the Na+/K+/2Clcarrier system. It increases urinary excretion of sodium, chloride, and water without significantly altering glomerular filtration rate, renal plasma flow, or acid-base balance. The bioavailability of Demadex tablets is approximately 80%, with peak serum concentration reached within 1 hour after oral administration. Torsemide is extensively bound to plasma proteins (>99%) and is primarily cleared by hepatic metabolism (80%) and renal excretion (20%). Nonclinical Toxicology No overall increase in tumor incidence was observed in lifetime studies in rats and mice. High doses in animal studies have shown renal tubular injury and a slight increase in renal adenomas and carcinomas. Torsemide showed no mutagenic activity in various in vivo and in vitro tests. How Supplied Demadex tablets are available in 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, and 100 mg strengths. They can be taken at any time in relation to meals, and no special dosage adjustment is necessary for elderly patients.
